standard.title: Australians in the Second World War — Places and Experiences
standard.description: the places where Australians fought, and their perspectives and experiences during the Second World War, such as the fall of Singapore, prisoners of war (POWs), the Battle of Britain and Kokoda
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have studied the places and experiences of Australians during World War One, including Gallipoli, the Western Front, and the perspectives of soldiers and nurses.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students identify and evaluate the significance of the places where Australians fought in WWII, and analyse the perspectives and experiences of different groups including POWs.

nodes.label: Where Australians fought
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify the major theatres and locations where Australians fought in the Second World War and explain the strategic significance of each.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least three locations where Australians fought and explain the significance of at least one.
nodes.typical_width: Identify and evaluate the significance of the major theatres: North Africa (Tobruk), Malaya and Singapore, New Guinea (Kokoda, Milne Bay), Darwin, and the broader Pacific campaign; explain the strategic importance of each location to the overall Allied war effort.
wider: Investigate the significance of the North Africa campaign (Tobruk, El Alamein) as the theatre that first established Australia's WWII reputation, examining how 'the Rats of Tobruk' became a symbol of Australian resilience
Compare the strategic importance of the Pacific theatre locations from both Allied and Japanese perspectives, examining how geography shaped military decision-making

response_modes.reason: Students need a working spatial and strategic orientation to the war's geography before they can meaningfully analyse experiences. Map-based activities identifying theatres and their relationship to Australian territory (especially the threat to the mainland) build the necessary context.

success_criteria: Identify at least three locations where Australians fought and place them correctly in the European or Asia-Pacific theatre
Explain the strategic significance of at least one location in terms of what its loss or defence meant for the broader war
Describe the connection between the fall of Singapore and the threat to the Australian mainland

nodes.label: Kokoda and the Anzac legend
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can investigate the significance of the Kokoda campaign, explaining both its strategic importance and its contribution to Australian national identity.
nodes.minimum_width: Explain what was at stake strategically in the Kokoda campaign and describe why it became significant in Australian national memory.
nodes.typical_width: Investigate the Kokoda campaign — the Japanese advance along the Kokoda Track, the threat to Port Moresby, the role of Australian infantry and Papuan carriers, the turning of the Japanese advance; explain how Kokoda reinforced and extended the Anzac legend in the context of the Pacific War.
wider: Examine the role of the Fuzzy Wuzzy Angels (Papuan carriers) in the Kokoda campaign, analysing how their contribution has been acknowledged and sometimes marginalised in Australian memory of the campaign

Compare the construction of the Kokoda legend with the construction of the Gallipoli legend — examining what values each narrative emphasises and how each has been used in different historical periods
Investigate the historiography of Kokoda, examining how the campaign has been interpreted differently by military historians, nationalist writers, and postcolonial scholars

response_modes.reason: Kokoda is often taught as a standalone national legend; widening to include Papuan perspectives and comparative legend-building prevents exemplar convergence on a single nationalist narrative.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Kokoda's dual significance — strategic and legendary — makes it a productive site for examining how historical events become national myths, a transferable analytical skill relevant throughout the course.
success_criteria: Explain the strategic significance of the Kokoda campaign, including what a Japanese victory would have meant for Australia
Describe at least two features of the Kokoda campaign that contributed to its place in Australian national memory
Explain how Kokoda reinforced the Anzac legend, identifying at least one point of continuity with WWI memory

nodes.label: POW experiences and perspectives
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can compare the experiences and perspectives of different groups of prisoners of war, explaining how treatment varied and what this reveals about the nature of the conflict.
nodes.minimum_width: Compare the experiences of Australian POWs under German control with those under Japanese control, explaining at least two differences.
nodes.typical_width: Compare POW experiences across multiple contexts: those held by Germany (relatively governed by Geneva Convention) vs those held by Japan (Thai-Burma Railway, Ambon, Rabaul); examine specific groups including those used as forced labour on the Thai-Burma Railway and army nurses captured in Singapore; analyse what these experiences reveal about different ideological and cultural approaches to the treatment of prisoners.
wider: Examine the experiences of nurses captured at Singapore (such as the Bangka Island massacre) as a case study in how gender intersected with POW status, analysing perspectives that are often marginalised in mainstream WWII narratives
Investigate the long-term psychological and physical impacts of POW experiences, using oral histories or memoir sources to examine how survivors made sense of their experiences

Compare the treatment of POWs with the treatment of civilian internees (including Australian women and children interned in Japanese camps), examining the relationship between military and civilian captivity

response_modes.reason: Students often reduce POW experience to suffering without engaging with the analytical question of why treatment differed. Structure the comparison around specific criteria — adherence to Geneva Convention, use of forced labour, death rates — to build analytical rather than purely empathetic responses.

Extending beyond the Thai-Burma Railway (the default exemplar) to include Ambon, Rabaul, and Singapore nurses broadens the range of POW experiences students understand and prevents a single narrative dominating.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The POW comparison offers a productive opportunity to examine how ideology, culture, and international law interact — and how marginalised perspectives (nurses, civilian internees, Papuan auxiliaries) complicate the dominant combat narrative.
success_criteria: Compare the experiences of Australian POWs under German and Japanese control, identifying at least two significant differences
Describe the experiences of at least one specific group of POWs (e.g. those on the Thai-Burma Railway, nurses captured in Singapore) and explain what makes their experience historically significant
Explain what the treatment of POWs reveals about the ideological and cultural context of the Second World War
